prompt: Render a polished, buildable native Windows 11 desktop app screen for Freehand, a tray-first local dictation utility. Landscape 3:2 composition, crisp readable UI text, app filling the frame, Windows minimize/maximize/close controls at top right. This is an actual working product concept, not a marketing page or design presentation. Use familiar native buttons, inputs, navigation and icons. Dark appearance. Real navigation labels: History, Dictionary, Settings. Search history scopes only the history. Synthetic sample transcripts, shared across concepts: Today 10:42: "Keep the input device selected while recording. If the microphone disconnects, preserve the recording and offer Retry." Today 10:18: "The settings change should take effect after the current recording finishes." Yesterday 16:05: "Review the dictionary corrections before the next release." Actions are Copy and Delete. No usage metrics or invented features. A small floating status pill at the bottom center shows a red recording dot, a restrained white waveform, "Recording", and "00:12". It is secondary to the window content. No tagline or explanatory helper copy. Lead with a familiar Windows navigation sidebar and an expansive full-width history area. The sidebar is visibly labeled Freehand, History selected, Dictionary, Settings. The main area has a clean History heading and search field over dated full-width transcript rows, with two lines of readable text in each and a small Copy button for the selected row. No separate detail pane and no top tabs. Use the craft of Windows 11 Fluent: neutral charcoal shell, slightly lifted neutral content surface, near-white Segoe-style text, quiet blue selection and correctly scaled native controls. Keep hierarchy, spacing, edges and alignment meticulous. Its identifying move is a restrained selected-row treatment continuous across the history width. The result is an understated daily utility that feels familiar on Windows. No decorative acrylic glow, no heavy borders, no nested card containers, no cassette or hardware metaphor.
